name: Colistin
route_note: IV (or IM) as the prodrug colistimethate sodium with loading dose; nebulised colistimethate in cystic fibrosis; oral colistin sulfate for selective gut decontamination; topical/otic preparations.
targets: Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane

discovery.note: Isolated in Japan from Paenibacillus (then Bacillus) polymyxa var. colistinus; reported in 1950. Colistin and colistimethate became available for clinical use in 1959.

tagline: Old polymyxin revived as a last-resort drug against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negatives
summary: Colistin (polymyxin E) is a cationic lipopeptide antibiotic discovered in Japan in the late 1940s. Abandoned in the 1970s for nephro- and neurotoxicity, it returned as a last-line treatment for carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas and Enterobacterales, and plasmid mcr resistance genes discovered in 2015 have made it a symbol of the antimicrobial resistance crisis.
mechanism: Colistin's positively charged diaminobutyric acid residues displace calcium and magnesium bridging lipopolysaccharide molecules in the outer membrane; its fatty-acyl tail then inserts and disrupts both outer and inner membranes, causing leakage and death. It also binds and neutralises endotoxin.

Resistance arises when bacteria add phosphoethanolamine or 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose to lipid A, reducing its negative charge (via PmrAB/PhoPQ mutations, mgrB inactivation in Klebsiella, or plasmid mcr genes). Proteus, Serratia, Providencia and Burkholderia are intrinsically resistant, and it has no Gram-positive activity.
uses: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacterales infections, usually in combination
Chronic Pseudomonas lung infection in cystic fibrosis (inhaled)
Selective digestive decontamination in intensive care (some countries)

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Koyama and colleagues isolate colistin from a Japanese soil bacterium.

history.title: Clinical use
history.detail: Colistin and colistimethate enter clinical use in the late 1950s, including in the US as Coly-Mycin.

history.title: Decline
history.detail: Reports of nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity, and the arrival of aminoglycosides, lead to colistin falling out of systemic use during the 1970s.

history.title: Revival
history.detail: Spread of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas prompts renewed IV use in the 2000s.

history.title: mcr-1 discovered
history.detail: Plasmid-mediated colistin resistance gene mcr-1 is reported in E. coli from pigs, meat and patients in China (Lancet Infectious Diseases, published 2016).

history.title: Animal growth-promoter ban
history.detail: China bans colistin as a growth promoter in animal feed.

history.title: International consensus
history.detail: International guidelines on optimal polymyxin dosing recommend loading doses and therapeutic monitoring where possible.

pk.half_life: colistin about 9–14 hours after IV colistimethate (prolonged in renal impairment)
pk.metabolism: colistimethate is hydrolysed to active colistin; colistin undergoes non-renal clearance

serious: Neurotoxicity, including neuromuscular blockade and respiratory arrest

facts: Doses of colistimethate are expressed variously as international units or as colistin base activity, a long-standing source of dosing confusion.
Colistin is classified in the WHO 'Reserve' antibiotic group.
